intuition: Move the tail to the front k times, finding the tail on each pass: O(nk). Modulo and one cut avoid repeated traversals. Huge rotation counts repeat the same arrangements, so simulating every step ignores the periodic structure.

The last k nodes become a prefix while their relative order stays unchanged. After reducing k modulo length, only one boundary moves: the edge between the original prefix and suffix. Closing the old tail-to-head link temporarily removes the special end of the list. The new tail is then found by position, and cutting after it restores a linear list. This method rewires existing nodes rather than copying their values into a separate container.

The new tail is the last node of the original prefix of length n-k. Its successor is the first node of the original suffix. Closing the old tail-to-head edge concatenates suffix and prefix; cutting after the new tail preserves every node once in the required order. Two scans locate the old and new tails; existing nodes are reused.

steps: Count five nodes and find old tail value 5.
Reduce k=2 modulo 5; two nodes should move from the end to the front.
Connect 5.next to the original head 1, creating a temporary circle.
Walk length-k-1=2 links from 1 to new tail 3; new head is its successor 4.

codeNotes.note: A complete revolution changes nothing; this prevents billion-step traversal for a large rotation count.
Joining the original ends allows the suffix to continue directly into the original prefix.
Breaking this precise edge both produces the correct boundary and prevents returning a cyclic list.
